Slides accessible here: `https://pengyunc.quarto.pub/week10/` ## This tutorial: Prediction Interval Estimation {auto-animate="true"} In this tutorial we use simulation to understand and explore the methods for prediction interval calculation.
:::{.callout-note title="Activities"} - Exercises 1 & 2: Simulating 95% prediction intervals — coverage and average length (width) - Exercise 3: Investigating the effect of model misspecification on prediction interval properties - Exercise 4: Simulating prediction intervals with non-normal disturbances ::: ## Recap: Prediction Intervals {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} - Consider an AR(1) model and assume $Y_{n+1}$ has conditional distribution: $$ Y_{n+1} = \phi_{1}Y_{n} + U_{n+1} \quad \text{and} \quad Y_{n+1}\mid \mathscr{Y}_{t} \sim \mathrm{N}(\phi_{1}Y_{n}, \sigma_{n}^{2}) $$ $$ \color{blue}{\implies\quad \sigma_{n}^{2}=\operatorname{var}(Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n}) = \operatorname{var}(U_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})} $$ where $U_{t+1}$ is the 1-step-ahead prediction error. ::: :::{.fragment} - The 95% confidence interval for $(Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})$ is: $$\phi_{1}Y_{n}\pm 1.96\times \sigma_{n}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} - It follows that the 95\% prediction interval for $Y_{n+1}$ is: $$\quad\quad\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}Y_{t}\color{black}{\,\pm\, 1.96\times\,}\color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}_{n}}\color{black}\quad\text{where}\quad \begin{aligned}\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}&\color{purple}{\text{ is the usual parameter estimate}}\\ \color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}}&\color{teal}{=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=2}\hat{U}_{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}$$ assuming $\operatorname{var}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})$ is constant for all $t$. ::: ## Recap: Prediction Intervals {auto-animate="true"} - It follows that the 95\% prediction interval for $Y_{n+1}$ is: $$\quad\quad\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}Y_{n}\color{black}{\,\pm\, 1.96\times\,}\color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}_{n}}\color{black}\quad\text{where}\quad \begin{aligned}\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}&\color{purple}{\text{ is the usual parameter estimate}}\\ \color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}}&\color{teal}{=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=2}\hat{U}_{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}$$ assuming $\operatorname{var}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})$ is constant for all $t$. :::{.fragment} - This prediction interval contains $Y_{n+1}$ with approximately 95% probability in repeated samples. $\to$ we will illustrate this with a simulation ::: :::{.fragment} - This probability is understood in the frequentist sense: - given repeated drawings from the “population” of the data, the proportion of the constructed intervals will include actual $Y_t$ is 95%. ::: :::{.fragment} - Precision: A narrower prediction interval indicates a more precise forecast. ::: ## Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.callout-tip title="Code Outline"} :::{.incremental} - Repeat the following experiment `reps=1000` times: - Generate $200+12$ draws of $U_t$ from $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$ - Simulate $200+12$ observations from the AR(1) process - Withhold the final 12 observations as test set - Estimate the AR(1) model with the training set - Compute and store the upper and lower bounds of 95% PI for $h=1,2,\dots,12$ - Check whether the true values are contained within the 95% PIs - **Exercise 1:** Compute the probability at which the 95% PIs contains the true $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,2,\dots,12$ - **Exercise 2:** Compute the average lengths of the 95% PIs for each $h=1,2,\dots,12$ ::: ::: ## Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.panel-tabset} ## Initialisation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forecast) set.seed(30004) # For reproducibility reps <- 1000 n <- 200 # Estimation sample size per experiment hmax <- 12 # Forecast horizon ar <- 0.8 # AR(1) true coefficient # Storage for inclusion indicators Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) # Storage for length of each interval Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) ``` ::: ## Simulation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (r in 1:reps){ U <- rnorm(n+hmax) # N(0,1) prediction errors Y <- arima.sim(n=n+hmax, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) # Simulate data Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+hmax)] # Forecast sample Y <- Y[1:n] # Estimation sample # Estimate AR(1) model and generate forecasts and PIs eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] # lower bound of 95% PIs Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] # upper bound of 95% PIs Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) # Check inclusion Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Lengths of PIs } ``` ::: ## Extracting PIs Explained ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) print(eqf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Point Forecast Lo 80 Hi 80 Lo 95 Hi 95 201 1.28083447 0.04063708 2.521032 -0.6158838 3.177553 202 0.92003622 -0.64180357 2.481876 -1.4685916 3.308664 203 0.64385306 -1.07877267 2.366479 -1.9906756 3.278382 204 0.43244089 -1.37777477 2.242657 -2.3360451 3.200927 205 0.27060950 -1.58901411 2.130233 -2.5734394 3.114658 206 0.14673111 -1.74124272 2.034705 -2.7406757 3.034138 207 0.05190492 -1.85248483 1.956295 -2.8606079 2.964418 208 -0.02068246 -1.93462581 1.893261 -2.9478062 2.906441 209 -0.07624651 -1.99576576 1.843273 -3.0118979 2.859405 210 -0.11877958 -2.04155854 1.803999 -3.0594162 2.821857 211 -0.15133771 -2.07602417 1.773349 -3.0948916 2.792216 212 -0.17626025 -2.10206353 1.749543 -3.1215222 2.769002 ``` ::: :::

Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.panel-tabset} ## Exercise 1 - Coverage :::{.callout-question} Compute the probabilities at which the 95% PIs contains the true $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$. :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Coverage <- apply(Included, 2, mean) * 100 names(Coverage) <- paste0("h=", 1:hmax) print(Coverage) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 94.4 93.3 94.7 93.5 92.9 92.3 94.4 93.9 94.7 93.9 93.5 93.2 ``` ::: :::
The simulated coverages are slightly below 95%? - arises partly because of simulation error (only 1000 simulations) - also partly because the forecast intervals are based on model estimates from $n=200$ sample sizes which do not yield the exact model coefficients. ## Exercise 2 - Lengths :::{.callout-question} Compute the average lengths of the 95% PIs for each $h=1,2,\dots,12$. :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean), 2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=", 1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 3.92 4.98 5.54 5.87 6.06 6.19 6.26 6.31 6.35 6.37 6.38 6.39 ``` ::: :::
- The average length of the interval is increasing in $h$, which reflects the formula we have seen in lectures for the variances for $h$-step-ahead forecasts. $$\textstyle\operatorname{var}(U_{t\mid t-h})=\sum^{h-1}_{j=0}\phi_{1}^{2j}\sigma^{2}\qquad\color{teal}{\boxed{\leftarrow\;\textsf{\small{}From Lecture 9}\;}}$$ - Intuition: it is *more difficult* to forecast further into the future. ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Now change the simulation to demonstrate the effects of model misspecification on the properties of the prediction intervals. $\to$ **Simulate AR(1) data, but forecast with MA(1)** What are the implications for the prediction intervals? Explain the results for the lengths of the prediction intervals for $h>1$. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## Initialisation Code Code for initialisation is the same as in Exercises 1 and 2. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(30004) # For reproducibility reps <- 1000 n <- 200 # Estimation sample size per experiment hmax <- 12 # Forecast horizon ar <- 0.8 # AR(1) true coefficient # Storage for inclusion indicators Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) # Storage for length of each interval Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) ``` ::: ## Estimation Code The only change is to the estimation command, replacing AR(1) with MA(1). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (r in 1:reps){ U <- rnorm(n+hmax) # N(0,1) prediction errors Y <- arima.sim(n=n+hmax, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) # Simulate data Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+hmax)] # Forecast sample Y <- Y[1:n] # Estimation sample # Estimate MA(1) model and generate forecasts and PIs eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(0,0,1)) ### <- MISSPECIFIED!!! eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] # lower bound of 95% PIs Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] # upper bound of 95% PIs Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) # Check inclusion Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Lengths of PIs } ``` :::
## Results: Coverage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Coverage: proportion of inclusion at each h Coverage <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 names(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(Coverage) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 93.0 89.6 89.8 89.6 89.1 89.2 90.9 89.6 90.3 89.9 89.5 89.2 ``` ::: :::
When the model is misspecified: - the coverage rates of the prediction intervals decrease below 90% as $h$ increases. - the true value is included within the interval less frequently than the desired 90%. ## Results: Lengths ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
The average lengths of the 95% PIs are the same for $h=2,\dots,12$. ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.fragment} :::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ ::: :::
:::{.fragment} When $h=1$: $$Y_{t+1}=U_{t+1}+\theta_{1}U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1})=0}+\theta_{1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=u_t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$$ where $u_{t}$ is the realised value of $U_t$ (it is a constant). ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$: Mean of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$. :::{.fragment}
How about the variance? ::: :::{.center} [$\displaystyle\operatorname{var}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1})=\sigma^{2}}+\underbrace{\;\;\operatorname{var}(\theta_{1}U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})\;\;}_{=0,\; \theta_{1}u_{t}\text{ is a constant}}$]{.fragment}[$=\sigma^{2}$]{.fragment} ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$: Mean of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$. Variance of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\operatorname{var}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\sigma^{2}$ :::{.fragment}
Given that $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}=U_{t+1}+\theta_{1}u_{t}$ and $U_{t+1}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$, ::: :::{.center} [$\implies Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(\theta_{1}u_{t},\sigma^{2})\quad$]{.fragment} [$\color{teal}{\implies \textsf{the 95\% PI is}\quad \hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}}$]{.fragment} ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$, the 95% prediction interval is $\hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}$. [When $h=2$,]{.fragment} [we have $Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}=U_{t+2}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}$.]{.fragment} :::{.incremental} - **Mean:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+2})=0}+\theta_{1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1})=0}=0$ - **Variance:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathrm{var}(Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(U_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\operatorname{var}(U_{t+2})=\sigma^{2}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(\theta_{1}U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\theta_{1}^{2}\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1})=\theta_{1}^{2}\sigma^{2}}=(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2}$ - **95% PI:** $\;\;$Since $Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2})\;\;\implies\;\; 0\pm1.96\times \sqrt{(1+\hat{\theta}_{1}^{2})\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$
::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$, the 95% prediction interval is $\hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}$. When $h\ge 2$, we have $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}=U_{t+h}+\theta_{1}U_{t+h-1}$. - **Mean:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+h})=0}+\theta_{1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+h-1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+h-1})=0}=0$ - **Variance:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathrm{var}(Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(U_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\operatorname{var}(U_{t+h})=\sigma^{2}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(\theta_{1}U_{t+h-1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\theta_{1}^{2}\operatorname{var}(U_{t+h-1})=\theta_{1}^{2}\sigma^{2}}=(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2}$ - **95% PI:** $\;\;$Since $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2})\;\;\implies\;\; 0\pm1.96\times \sqrt{(1+\hat{\theta}_{1}^{2})\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$ ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 4.76 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 5.65 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$, the 95% prediction interval is $\hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}$. When $h\ge 2$, the 95% prediction interval is $0\pm 1.96\times\sqrt{(1+\hat{\theta}_{1}^{2})\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$.
[Applying an MA(1) model produces prediction intervals of equal length for every $h>1$.]{.fragment} [The fact that the MA(1) model is misspecified in this case does not change its formula for calculation.]{.fragment} ## Exercise 4(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## True DGP - We know that when $X\sim\chi_{k}^{2}$, $\mathbb{E}(X)=k$ and $\operatorname{var}(X)=2k$. - To standardise it (mean 0 and unit variance), we can take the "z-score": $$U=\frac{X-\mathbb{E}(X)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(X)}}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ - The true DGP is: $$Y_{t}=\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\textsf{where}\quad \color{blue}{\underbrace{\;\;U_{t}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}\quad\textsf{and}\quad X\sim\chi_{1}^{2}\;\;}_{\chi^{2}_{1}\textsf{ centered to have mean 0}}}$$ ## PDF Shape ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- seq(-1, 5, length.out = 500) # support starts at -1 y <- dchisq(x + 1, df = 1) # density of χ²(1), shifted plot(x, y, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, main = "", ylab = "", xlab = "", ylim = c(0, 1.5)) abline(h = 0, lty = 2) # horizontal line at 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ECOM30004_Tutorial_10_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Full Code The following code took me around 27 minutes and 10 seconds to run (on a 2025 MacBook Pro, 5 minutes slower than David's "unremarkable 2011 MacBook Pro").
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forecast) reps <- 1000 n <- 200 h <- 12 arv <- c(0.3,0.6,0.9) Coverage <- matrix(nrow=length(arv), ncol=h) colnames(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:h) rownames(Coverage) <- paste0("ar=",arv) CoverageBS <- Coverage AvgLength <- Coverage AvgLengthBS <- Coverage et<- system.time( for (ac in 1:length(arv)){ ar <- arv[ac] Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) IncludedBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) LengthBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) set.seed(3400) for (r in 1:reps){ # Simulate time series U <- ((rnorm(n+h))^2-1)/sqrt(2) Y <- arima.sim(n=n+h, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+h)] Y <- Y[1:n] # AR(1) estimation eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) # Normal prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Bootstrap prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h, bootstrap=TRUE) LowerBS <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] UpperBS <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] IncludedBS[r,] <- 1*(LowerBSYf) LengthBS[r,] <- UpperBS-LowerBS } Coverage[ac,] <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 CoverageBS[ac,] <- apply(IncludedBS, 2, mean)*100 AvgLength[ac,] <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) AvgLengthBS[ac,] <- round(apply(LengthBS, 2, mean),2) }) ``` :::
## Result - Coverage ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(Coverage) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 95 94.4 92.8 93.4 94.9 96.0 94.9 95.0 93.3 94.0 94.2 94.7 ar=0.6 94 94.4 94.4 94.2 94.2 94.3 94.3 94.6 95.4 94.3 96.0 95.1 ar=0.9 94 93.9 93.2 94.3 93.0 94.8 93.8 94.4 93.7 94.4 93.2 93.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} print(CoverageBS) # Bootstrapped ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 94.5 93.3 93.8 93.4 95.5 95.3 94.7 93.4 93.0 94.4 94.5 94.0 ar=0.6 94.3 93.1 93.9 93.9 92.6 92.5 93.2 93.6 94.6 94.0 93.7 92.4 ar=0.9 93.5 92.5 92.2 92.9 92.0 92.9 91.8 92.1 91.3 93.0 92.6 93.4 ``` ::: :::
- The coverage results are very similar across the boards. - Note: Remember these are just simulation estimates from only 1000 replications, and don't over-interpret small differences. - Nevertheless there might be a slight deficiency of about 1% in the coverage of the bootstrap intervals relative to the normal intervals when $\phi=0.9$. - Otherwise, there is little to choose between the two intervals on this criterion. - This is quite interesting because theoretically the bootstrap intervals are valid in this case but the normal intervals are not. - Note: CLT does not provide an approximation for non-normal data when computing prediction intervals. ## Result - Lengths ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(AvgLength) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 3.90 4.06 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 4.08 ar=0.6 3.91 4.54 4.75 4.82 4.85 4.86 4.86 4.87 4.87 4.87 4.87 4.87 ar=0.9 3.91 5.22 6.05 6.64 7.07 7.39 7.64 7.83 7.98 8.10 8.20 8.27 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} print(AvgLengthBS) # Bootstrapped ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 3.61 3.81 3.86 3.86 3.87 3.85 3.86 3.87 3.86 3.86 3.86 3.86 ar=0.6 3.62 4.28 4.53 4.63 4.66 4.68 4.69 4.70 4.69 4.69 4.70 4.70 ar=0.9 3.62 4.93 5.80 6.41 6.86 7.19 7.45 7.65 7.82 7.94 8.04 8.13 ``` ::: :::
The bootstrap intervals can be as much as 10% shorter for small $h$, although this advantage reduces to 5% or less as $h$ increases. ::: ## Exercise 4(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. :::
**Overall:** :::{.incremental} - There are not major differences between the two intervals and the choice would be subjective. - The advantage in length may suggest some *weak preference* for the bootstrap intervals in this particular model. ::: ## Exercise 4(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (b) The second distribution for $U_t$ is the $t$ distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## True DGP The true DGP is: $$Y_{t}=\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\textsf{where}\quad \color{blue}{U_{t}\sim t_{4}}$$ This distribution has fatter tails (higher kurtosis) than $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000) y_t <- dt(x, df = 4) y_norm <- dnorm(x) plot(x, y_t, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 0.45), ylab = "", xlab = "", main = "") lines(x, y_norm, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2) abline(h = 0, lty = 3) legend("topright", legend = c("t (df=4)", "Normal(0,1)"), col = c("red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ECOM30004_Tutorial_10_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Full Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forecast) reps <- 1000 n <- 200 h <- 12 arv <- c(0.3,0.6,0.9) Coverage <- matrix(nrow=length(arv), ncol=h) colnames(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:h) rownames(Coverage) <- paste0("ar=",arv) CoverageBS <- Coverage AvgLength <- Coverage AvgLengthBS <- Coverage et<- system.time( for (ac in 1:length(arv)){ ar <- arv[ac] Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) IncludedBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) LengthBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) set.seed(3400) for (r in 1:reps){ # Simulate time series U <- rt(n=n+h, df=4) Y <- arima.sim(n=n+h, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+h)] Y <- Y[1:n] # AR(1) estimation eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) # Normal prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Bootstrap prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h, bootstrap=TRUE) LowerBS <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] UpperBS <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] IncludedBS[r,] <- 1*(LowerBSYf) LengthBS[r,] <- UpperBS-LowerBS } Coverage[ac,] <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 CoverageBS[ac,] <- apply(IncludedBS, 2, mean)*100 AvgLength[ac,] <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) AvgLengthBS[ac,] <- round(apply(LengthBS, 2, mean),2) }) ``` :::
::: {.cell} ::: ## Result - Coverage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(Coverage) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 94.9 95.0 94.8 94.0 94.6 94.8 93.3 94.0 94.5 94.4 95.9 94.2 ar=0.6 95.2 93.8 94.2 93.6 92.1 94.5 95.2 94.0 94.0 94.9 93.6 93.5 ar=0.9 94.6 95.4 93.7 93.4 93.4 93.4 93.4 91.3 91.5 90.8 91.0 90.8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} print(CoverageBS) # Bootstrapped ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 94.8 94.6 95.0 94.1 94.3 94.8 93.5 94.2 94.3 94.5 95.4 93.6 ar=0.6 95.7 94.3 93.5 93.4 92.5 94.4 95.3 94.2 93.7 94.6 93.3 93.9 ar=0.9 94.2 95.4 93.8 93.7 92.9 93.1 93.0 91.1 91.3 90.2 90.4 90.1 ``` ::: :::
**Comments:** - One finding to note is that the coverage properties deteriorate for larger $h$ when $\phi_{1}=0.9$. - The finite sample statistical properties of prediction with strong autocorrelation (i.e., large $\phi_{1}$) can require larger samples for the asymptotic properties (i.e. 95% coverage) to apply.
## Result - Lengths ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(AvgLength) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 5.48 5.71 5.73 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 5.74 ar=0.6 5.45 6.32 6.60 6.70 6.74 6.76 6.76 6.76 6.77 6.77 6.77 6.77 ar=0.9 5.52 7.35 8.50 9.31 9.89 10.33 10.66 10.92 11.12 11.28 11.40 11.50 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} print(AvgLengthBS) # Bootstrapped ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` h=1 h=2 h=3 h=4 h=5 h=6 h=7 h=8 h=9 h=10 h=11 h=12 ar=0.3 5.54 5.77 5.80 5.80 5.79 5.81 5.79 5.80 5.80 5.80 5.80 5.80 ar=0.6 5.56 6.43 6.72 6.81 6.85 6.86 6.87 6.87 6.86 6.85 6.86 6.87 ar=0.9 5.55 7.44 8.64 9.46 10.06 10.56 10.90 11.13 11.33 11.47 11.59 11.69 ``` ::: :::
The average lengths of the prediction intervals increases with $h$ and $\phi_{1}$ (the same applied in part a) $\implies$ Long-horizon prediction is more difficult when time series are more strongly autocorrelated.
## Conclusion - Overall, there is no advantage to be found for the bootstrap intervals in this model. If anything they are slightly longer. - Despite the non-normality, the normal prediction intervals work quite well in this case. - This could be due to the shape of non-normality is different in this case, as the distribution is symmetric. ::: ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
